# Closing: What to Keep {#sec-what-to-keep}

Nine papers, four parts, and a set of constructed devices. This chapter says what survives.

Three sections. the structure the book has been building, the things the three authors agree
about and the things they do not, and what a reader should do with any of it.

## The three-layer structure

The book's material arranges itself into three layers, and each constrains the next in one
direction only.

**The worldview layer asks what kind of world this is.** Shape first. Thin or fat tailed, stationary or not,
independent or long-memoried. This layer constrains which models can be used, because a model
premised on a light tail is not a candidate in a heavy-tailed world regardless of how well it fits.

**The epistemology layer asks what can be known.** Then knowledge. Existence, estimability, and the sampling limits
on detecting skill. This layer constrains how much can be staked, because a stake is a claim on
knowledge, and the knowledge may not be available.

**The action layer asks what to do.** Action last. Screening irreversible exposures, choosing the form of the
output, sizing with a discount. This layer constrains which opportunities are worth pursuing.

The constraint runs downward. Only downward. **A worldview judgement rules out models; a knowledge judgement rules
out stakes; an action judgement rules out opportunities.**

The reverse direction is a test rather than a constraint, and it is the more useful half. **If a
proposed model requires a light tail, ask what the worldview layer says about tails. If a proposed
stake requires a precise estimate, ask what the epistemology layer says about precision. If a
proposed opportunity requires an irreversible exposure, ask what the action layer says about
reversibility.**

That test is the practical content of the whole book, and it fits in a sentence: **when something
requires what an earlier layer denies, the something is wrong.**

## What happens if you learn only one of them

The three authors overlap substantially and diverge on important points, and a reader who studies one
and skips the others inherits a specific distortion.

**Mandelbrot alone** gives the shape of the problem and no guidance on action. A reader who stops
here has a vocabulary for tails and no procedure, and is likely to conclude that measurement is
impossible — which is the over-reading Chapter 7 documented. **The missing piece is Thorp's
demonstration that in a computable setting, an edge exists and can be sized.**

**Taleb alone** gives the survival rules and the caution, plus a polemical edge that makes strong
claims easy to over-apply. A reader who stops here will screen everything, run nothing, and find
precaution everywhere. **The missing piece is Mandelbrot's insistence that the tail has a shape, which
is what makes measurement possible in a bounded range, and Thorp's demonstration that a
probabilistic edge can be found and used.**

**Thorp alone** gives the operational method and the sizing rules, in a register so practical that the
premises disappear. A reader who stops here will size carefully on the basis of edges that may not
exist, because the calculability of the casino has been generalised into a world where the edge must
be estimated. **The missing piece is Mandelbrot's warning about what the estimates can carry and
Taleb's insistence that the fourth quadrant is different in kind.**

| Only this author | You gain | You are left believing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mandelbrot | The shape of the problem | Nothing can be measured |
| Taleb | The survival rules | Nothing should be attempted |
| Thorp | The operational method | Everything can be estimated |

**The three distortions are not random. Each is the shape of one author's contribution taken as a
complete account.**

## What they agree on

Five points, and they are the book's most defensible content because three authors working from
different methods reached them.

**Distribution shape matters more than central tendency.** All three agree. None of the three treats an average as the
primary object.

**Summary statistics have domains of validity.** All three agree. None treats a variance, an expectation, or a
correlation as universally meaningful.

**Ruin is different in kind from loss.** All three agree. All three treat the absorbing state as categorically
separate, and none attempts to price it.

**The estimation problem is central rather than incidental.** All three agree. Mandelbrot showed it for exponents,
Taleb for the fourth quadrant, Thorp for the parameters of his own criterion.

**Survival constraints come before optimisation.** All three agree. The ordering of Chapter 29 is a formalisation of
something all three practice.

## Where they disagree

Three disagreements. Stated, not resolved.

**Whether the world is fundamentally unmeasurable or merely hard to measure.** Mandelbrot's programme
sought a better description; Taleb's mature position is closer to a limit on what description can
accomplish. **The difference matters because it determines whether research is the right response to
uncertainty.**

**Whether optimisation is available at all.** Thorp optimises a fraction and describes the result as
a practical tool. Taleb's anti-optimisation stance treats the search for an optimum as a source of
fragility. **Chapter 21's discount is an attempt at a middle position, and a reader who finds it
unsatisfying is in good company: the two authors would not agree with each other either.**

**How much weight to put on the most extreme outcomes.** Mandelbrot's mathematics gives tails a
structure and quantifies them. Taleb's fourth quadrant treats the extreme as the case that decides,
and treats quantification of it as unreliable. **The book has followed each where its material
demanded, which is not the same as resolving the difference.**

## How to use the book

Three suggestions, in order of how much they ask.

**Use the ordering as a checklist.** Three questions. Three questions, in order, before any number is computed. The
first one costs minutes and requires no data.

**Use the registers.** They are separate on purpose. The verification file and the construction file are separate on purpose. Any
claim in this book that is not in the first was not verified, and every device in Part IV is in the
second, which means none of them has been tested.

**Check the fourth column.** Including here. For anything you read — here or elsewhere — ask who benefits if it is
believed, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong. **The book's own constructions are in
that set, including its central one.**

## The closing rule

The one sentence worth carrying out of this book is not about tails or sizing.

**For any judgement you read, first ask who bears the consequences.**

An author writing about a risk they do not take is producing description. A practitioner who takes it
is producing a decision under a constraint the author did not face. **The two can agree on every
proposition and differ in what they say, because one is describing and the other is choosing.**

This is not an argument against theory. It is an argument for reading the consequences column. The
nine papers in this book are worth reading because their authors, in different ways, faced them:
Mandelbrot measuring a market he did not trade, Taleb taking positions on the risk he described,
Thorp computing an edge he then staked money on.

## What remains unverified

The book's registers record the following classes of entry, and a reader who wants to know the
evidential status of any claim should consult them.

**Verified metadata** — bibliographic facts, checked against databases.

**Verified via text** — claims read in the source or in an accessible version of it.

**Verified via secondary source** — claims described at one remove, with the remove stated.

**Constructed** — the book's own devices, none of them tested.

**Unverified, and deliberately uncited** — items that would have strengthened the argument and could
not be checked. Several are named in the chapters where they would have appeared.

**The registers are the book's own audit.** They include the entries that weaken it.

## Claim and tool

The claim: the material arranges into three layers with one-way constraints, and the three authors
agree on five points and disagree on three.

The tool: the reverse test — when something requires what an earlier layer denies, it is wrong.

## The three layers as a reading order

The layers were presented as a structure. They are also an order in which to read the material, and the
order differs from the book's own arrangement.

**First the epistemology. Fast.** What can be known: existence, estimability, sampling limits. This is
Part I plus the grid, and it is available from about forty pages of primary material. A reader who
understands only this layer will not be misled by a point estimate again.

**Then the action layer. Slower.** What to do: screen irreversibility, choose the output form, size with
a discount. This is Parts II and III, and it takes longer because it requires practice rather than
reading. The ninety-minute exercise of Chapter 27 is the fastest route in.

**Finally the worldview layer. Slowest.** What kind of world this is: tails, memory, stationarity. This
is the hardest layer, it is the most contested, and it is also the one whose conclusions are least
necessary for practical decisions, because the structural screening does not depend on them.

**Why the order is reversed relative to the book.** The book proceeds from the world to the decision,
because the argument runs that way. A reader with a decision to make should proceed from what can be
known to what to do, and can leave the worldview questions for later.

**What a reader loses by taking this order.** The appreciation of why the structural devices exist — the
tail arguments are their foundations. A practitioner who skips the worldview layer will use the devices
correctly without being able to defend them, which is adequate for personal decisions and insufficient
for teaching.


## The book's own failure conditions, in one place

The closing chapter of a book that insists on refutation conditions should carry its own. Four, stated
plainly.

**If the papers' claims were not weakened.** The whole arrangement rests on the pattern of claims
weakening while tools survive. A reader who checks the verification register and finds the claims
standing is entitled to dismiss the framing, and the register is designed to permit exactly that check.

**If the structural screen does not change decisions.** Part IV exists because screening is claimed to
alter which options are on the table. Where it usually does not, the method is overhead.

**If the devices cannot be used badly, or cannot be used well.** A device with unreachable refutation
conditions is not testable, and a device whose correct use cannot be distinguished from its misuse by
anyone outside the room is not a device but a vocabulary.

**If the reader's situation fails a premise.** Which premise fails is the test given in the previous
chapter. **A book that tells you when to put it down has done more than one that does not.**

**What the book asks of a reader.** One check and one exercise. Check the verification register against
a source. Run the ninety-minute procedure on a live decision. Both take under two hours in total, and
either is enough to establish whether the material is worth more of the reader's time.


## The one-page version of the whole book

A reader who wants the argument in a single page, without the nine papers.

**On the world.** Three graded statements. Tails are thicker than the standard machinery assumes, the shape of the tail is
estimable only over a range, and some quantities that decision-makers rely on do not exist. **The three
statements are graded: the first is robust, the second is measured, the third is contested at its
boundary.**

**On knowledge.** Precision is not status. An estimate's precision is not its evidential status. Two estimators that disagree by
more than the decision's tolerance leave the quantity unusable whatever the standard error says, and the
most consequential features of a distribution are the least well estimated by construction, because they
live in the rare events.

**On action.** Three stages. In order. Screen irreversible exposures first, because the screening requires no data and removes the
options that could end the sequence. Then determine whether the quantities exist and can be estimated. Only
then size, with a discount that reflects how well the edge is known.

**On edges.** Decaying assets. An edge is a decaying asset whose use contributes to its decay, and its discovery is a
research process rather than a purchase. Where the edge is estimated rather than computed, everything in
Parts I and III applies, including the arithmetic that says a decade of data is needed to detect a
plausible edge.

**On method.** One direction only. The three layers constrain one direction: the world constrains the models, the models
constrain the stakes, the stakes constrain the opportunities. **The test runs the other way: when something
requires what an earlier layer denies, the something is wrong.**

**On reading.** Four columns. A result decomposes into a claim, a tool, a vocabulary and a technique, and the four age
differently. Trust transfers from claim to tool over time, and the transfer should be deliberate. **The
question to carry away is not whether a judgement is true but who bears the consequences of its being
wrong.**

**What the page omits.** Every qualification, the registers, the refutation conditions of six constructed
devices, and the argument that the nine papers' claims were weakened while their tools survived. **The page
is a summary of a book whose central claim is that summaries lose the conditions, and it should be read
with that in mind.**


## What to do on Monday

The book closes with a reading rule and an argument. A reader who wants an action has this section, and it is
deliberately small.

**Three things, in order of cost.**

**Take one live decision and run stage one.** Exposures, mechanisms, stress-case exit costs, bounding moves.
**Ninety minutes, no data, and the output is a changed option set.**

**Take one quantity the decision depends on and write its defining expression.** Then ask whether it converges.
**Fifteen minutes, and the answer sometimes changes the method rather than the estimate.**

**Write down the coefficient of variation of the edge estimate, if there is one.** **The number forces the
judgement that the discount requires and that practitioners avoid.**

**What each produces.**

The first changes what is on the table. The second changes what kind of output is appropriate. The third changes
the size. **None requires the book's vocabulary, and none requires accepting any of its constructions.**

**What to do about the constructions themselves. One thing.** Attack one. Every device in Part IV is registered
with its refutation condition, and a reader who meets one has done the most useful thing the book makes
possible. **A proposal that survives an attempted refutation is worth more than one that is merely plausible,
and the attempt is the reader's contribution rather than the author's.**

**What not to do. Three things.**

Do not adopt the vocabulary without the questions. **Words without the discipline are what this book criticises
in the material it covers.**

Do not apply the procedure to reversible low-stakes decisions. **The overhead exceeds the benefit, and the
habit is worse than the overhead.**

Do not treat the devices as validated. **Nothing in the constructed register has been tested, and the register
says so on every row.**

**Why the list is short.** Because the book's central claim is about the conditions attached to claims, and a
closing list of actions that dropped the conditions would contradict it. **Three actions with their costs
stated, and the rest is reading.**


## The book in one table

A closing chapter that has argued for tables should end with one, and this is the book's whole apparatus on a
page.

| Question | The device | Where | What it returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Can this end the sequence? | Irreversibility ledger | 16, 27 | A bounded or reduced option set |
| Does the quantity exist? | Existence check | 13, 14 | A conditional statement, or a substitution |
| Can it be estimated? | Two-estimator comparison | 5, 14 | A cell, hence a method |
| What shape is my exposure? | Convexity audit | 15 | A sign, not a magnitude |
| Which method applies? | Four quadrants | 9 | A form of argument |
| Which matter does the claim survive? | The Constant's grades | 26 | A level, from I to III |
| What part of this do I keep? | Four-column protocol | 28 | A row, hence what to monitor |
| How much? | Discounted fraction | 20, 21 | A stake, a bound, or a refusal |
| In what order? | The ordering | 29 | The sequence itself |

**How to read the table. Downward.** Each row's answer determines which later rows apply. **A decision that ends
at row one needs nothing below it; one that reaches row eight has been screened twice and classified once.**

**What the table does not contain.** Any of the evidence. **The nine papers, the registers, and the arguments
that connect them are what the table presupposes, and the table is a map of the apparatus rather than of the
material.**

**What a reader should notice about the column headings.** Three of the nine rows return a non-numeric output:
an option set, a conditional statement, a sign. **Which is the book's substantive claim about decisions,
expressed as a table of outputs.**

**Why a table at the end rather than the beginning.** Because the devices were built in response to problems, and
a table presented first would look like a framework looking for applications. **Presented last, it is a summary
of nine responses to nine specific failures, which is what it is.**

**The one thing to do with it.** Take a live decision and walk down the rows, stopping where the answer becomes
determinate. **That is the ninety-minute procedure of Chapter 27, and the table is its index.**


## The three habits the book is trying to install

A book that ends with a reading rule and an argument should say what it hopes a reader will do without
thinking, because habits outlast rules.

**One. Ask whether the quantity exists.** Before precision, before method, before data. **The question costs
minutes and changes what the rest of the analysis can claim.**

**Two. Ask who bears the consequences.** Of any judgement, including the reader's own. **The question
separates description from decision and is the reason a practitioner's advice and an academic's advice can
differ while agreeing on every proposition.**

**Three. Ask what would have to stay the same.** Of any regularity being relied on. **Which converts an
assumption into a monitorable condition and gives the claim a duration.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** They are askable by someone who has read none of the book's
apparatus. **No registers, no vocabulary, no cells. Three questions and a minute.**

**How the habits differ from the rules.** A rule is applied deliberately; a habit is applied before the
deliberation starts. **The rules in this book need a page and a decision; the habits need a sentence and a
conversation.**

**What the habits cannot do.** Supply a method. **They identify which questions matter and leave the answering
to the apparatus, which is the right division: the questions are portable and the apparatus is not.**

**Why the book ends here rather than with the table.** Because the table is the book's apparatus and the
habits are its residue in a reader. **An apparatus can be adopted and abandoned; three questions installed in
a reader survive the book's arguments, including the ones that turn out to be wrong.**

**What a reader should do if they take nothing else.** Ask the three questions on the next decision. **Which
is a five-minute commitment and the only part of this material whose value does not depend on trusting the
author.**


## The three things that would change this book

A closing chapter that has argued for refutation conditions should say what would change the book itself, and
the three candidates are specific.

**One. A study of device use.** Coding a sample of applied risk analyses by which cell each quantity occupies,
and by whether the structural screening altered the decision. **Which would either support the book's central practical claim or show that the Replace cell is empty in practice, and it is the study the refutation sections keep asking for.**

**Two. A register of retired edges.** Lifetimes and mechanisms of death, by source. **Which would replace the chapter's reasoned durability ordering with a measured one, and it is the cheapest of the three for a firm to produce.**

**Three. A comparison of screened and unscreened decisions.** Where the procedure's recommendation differs from the ordinary one, and which was better over time. **Which is the sufficient condition the book admits it lacks, and which no amount of further reading in this material can supply.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each is empirical, each is cheap relative to the argument it
tests, and none has been run. **Which is the honest state of a book whose apparatus is checkable and whose
constructions are not.**

**What a reader can do about them. Two things.**

**Run the third on their own decisions.** Not as a study: as a practice. **A log of screened decisions with their outcomes is the individual version of the comparison.**

**Attack a device at its fourth field.** Which is the cheapest contribution and the one the registers are
built to receive.

**Why the book ends with its own refutation conditions rather than with a summary.** Because a summary would
imply the argument is closed, and it is not. **Three studies that would settle the questions the book raises,
named precisely enough to be run, which is the most a book of this kind can offer.**

**What the book claims about itself in closing. One sentence.** That nine results were weakened in their claims
while their tools survived, that structural screening changes decisions, and that the size of a position is
limited by how well its inputs are known. **Three claims, each with a stated test, and the tests are the
book's invitation.**


## The book's three questions and its one method

The closing chapter has collected habits, a table and refutation conditions. The minimum version is three
questions and one method, and it is worth stating as such.

**The questions.**

**Does the quantity exist.** Ask before precision, before method, before data.

**Who bears the consequences.** Ask of any judgement, including the reader's own.

**What would have to stay the same.** Ask of any regularity being relied on.

**The method.**

**Screen the irreversible exposures first.** Then classify the quantities. Then size, with a discount.

**Why three questions and one method rather than six devices.** Because the devices implement the method and
the questions test it. **A reader who has the questions can evaluate someone else's analysis; a reader who has
the method can produce one.**

**What the minimum leaves out. The apparatus.** The registers, the graders, the protocols. **Which are the
book's evidence rather than its advice, and a reader who takes the minimum has the advice.**

**Why the minimum is worth stating.** Because a book's practical content is what survives compression. **Three
questions, one method, and everything else in this book is the argument for why they are the right ones.**

**What the minimum cannot do. Settle anything.** The questions identify what matters and the method produces an
output. **Which is the correct division of labour and the reason the book ends with both.**

**How to test whether the minimum has been adopted. One observation.** Whether the questions are asked before
the method is applied. **Asked afterwards, they become a critique; asked first, they change what gets produced.**


## The book's claims and three grades

The closing chapter states three claims. Each has a grade, and the grades are what a reader should carry.

**The nine papers' claims were weakened while their tools survived.** Grade II. **Robust across the nine cases and
contested at its boundary, since the reading is the author's and the register is the evidence.**

**Structural screening changes decisions.** Grade II, and the weaker of the two. **Argued from the devices'
logic and from three constructed cases; the sufficient condition — that screened decisions are better over time —
is untested.**

**The size of a position is limited by how well its inputs are known.** Grade I in its arithmetic and II in its
application. **The interior optimum is a property of the objective function; the discount's form is a
proposal.**

**What the three grades imply for use. One instruction.** Rely on the third for the arithmetic, treat the first
two as arguments with their evidence attached, and attack the devices at their fourth fields. **Which is what the
book's four-column protocol would prescribe for any other work.**

**What a reader should notice about the three. One property.** The two grade II claims are the book's substantial
content and the grade I content is arithmetic borrowed from elsewhere. **Which is the honest description: the
book's contribution is two empirical readings and a set of constructions, and the arithmetic it uses is
standard.**

**Why stating the grades in closing is worth a section.** Because a reader who has followed nine weakened claims
deserves the same treatment applied to the book. **Three claims, three grades, and the grades are what a reader
carries when the arguments are no longer in front of them.**

**What would raise a grade. One thing per claim.** For the first, a check of the register entries against the
sources. For the second, the study the refutation sections keep naming. For the third, a derivation of the
discount rather than its proposal. **Three specific things, named, and none of them is reading more of this
book.**


## Boundary conditions

The three-layer structure is an organisation of this book's material, not a claim about how the three
authors saw their own work. None of them stated it in these terms.

The agreement and disagreement lists are the book's reading. A scholar of any of the three would
draw the lists differently, and the registers record which entries rest on the authors' own words and
which do not.

A last line. Ask the three questions. Run the one method. Write it down. Then decide. Nothing more is needed. Nothing less will do.
